title: New Construction Spray Foam Insulation
metaTitle: New Construction Spray Foam Insulation | St. George, UT Builders
metaDescription: Pre-drywall spray foam insulation for builders and GCs in Washington Fields, Little Valley, Desert Color, and Hurricane. Hit 2021 IECC Zone 3B code in one trade visit. Call 844-967-5247.
summary: Spray-foam-only pre-drywall insulation for St. George's new-home builders, delivering a code-exceeding, air-sealed envelope in a single coordinated trade visit.
intro: Washington County's new-home growth corridor isn't slowing down. Washington Fields, Little Valley, Desert Color, and Hurricane's expanding subdivisions are pulling framing crews, HVAC contractors, and insulation trades through tighter and tighter build schedules — and every one of those homes has to clear 2021 IECC Zone 3B inspection before drywall goes up. We work exclusively with builders and general contractors on pre-drywall spray foam installation, timed to your framing and HVAC rough-in sequence so the envelope is sealed, inspected, and ready for drywall without a schedule slip.

We're not a general insulation company that also does spray foam — spray foam is the only thing we do, which is why we do it better than anyone else in Washington County. That specialization matters most on new construction, where a mixed-material approach (batts in the walls, blown-in in the attic, separate air-sealing pass) means three trades touching the envelope and three chances for a gap, a compressed batt, or a missed penetration to fail blower-door testing. A single spray foam application seals the envelope and hits your R-value target in the same pass — one trade, one visit, one inspection-ready result.

St. George is a cooling-load-dominated desert climate, not a heating climate, and that changes what 'code minimum' should actually mean for a builder here. A roof deck under direct summer sun regularly hits 130-150°F, and every wall, ceiling, and rim joist gap you leave loose becomes a path for that heat to load onto the HVAC system the day the home is occupied. Spray foam's continuous air seal is what actually controls that heat gain — batt and blown-in insulation alone slow conduction but do very little to stop air infiltration, which is where most of the summer heat load and AC runtime comes from in this market. Builders who spec spray foam are building homes that perform better on day one, not just homes that pass inspection.

For builders, that translates directly into fewer buyer callbacks. A homebuyer who closes in April and hits their first 105°F stretch in June is going to notice if an upstairs bedroom over the garage runs hot or if the AC seems to run constantly. A properly sealed, foam-insulated envelope is the single biggest lever a builder has over that outcome, and it's a far cheaper problem to solve at the pre-drywall stage than to retrofit after a homeowner complaint six months into occupancy.

sections.heading: Built for the Pre-Drywall Sequence, Not Around It
body: New construction insulation only works on schedule if it's planned into the build sequence from the start, not squeezed in after framing and rough-in are already behind. We work directly with your superintendent or site lead to slot the spray foam application at the right point after framing inspection and HVAC/electrical/plumbing rough-in, and before drywall delivery. Because closed-cell and open-cell foam cure fast and don't require a multi-day dry-out window the way some site conditions demand, we can typically move a unit from foam-complete to drywall-ready faster than a batt-plus-blown-in sequence that needs separate crews for walls and attic.

On multi-lot subdivision phases, that consistency compounds. Every unit gets the same spec, the same application standard, and the same inspection-ready result, which means your super isn't troubleshooting a different insulation problem on lot 14 than lot 6.

We also plan around the realities of a live job site — material staging, ventilation requirements during cure time, and protecting adjacent finished work from overspray are all handled as standard practice, not as change-order line items. Our crews show up with a scope that matches what your framing package actually looks like on that lot, not a generic bid that assumes a different floor plan.

sections.heading: Hitting 2021 IECC Zone 3B in One Pass
body: St. George and Washington County build under the 2021 IECC as amended locally, and Zone 3B code minimums call for attic insulation in the R-38 to R-49 range and wall assemblies typically R-13 to R-21 depending on framing and cavity depth. We spec closed-cell foam (roughly R-6 to R-7 per inch) for roof decks, rim joists, and exterior-adjacent assemblies taking direct desert heat load, and open-cell foam (roughly R-3.5 to R-3.7 per inch) for standard interior wall cavities and non-roof-deck attic work, sizing thickness to clear your target R-value with margin, not exactly to the line.

Because spray foam is a monolithic air barrier as well as an insulator, it addresses both the R-value requirement and the air-leakage requirement in the same application — a distinction that matters more under the 2021 IECC's blower-door testing provisions than it did under older code cycles. A batt installation can hit the R-value on paper and still fail air-sealing inspection if the crew didn't hand-cut and seal every penetration around wiring, plumbing stacks, and top plates. Spray foam fills those gaps as part of the application, not as a separate remediation step.
bullets: Attic/roof-deck assemblies: closed-cell foam sized to R-38–R-49
Standard wall cavities: open-cell or closed-cell foam sized to R-13–R-21 by assembly
Rim joists and band joists: closed-cell foam as standard practice, not an optional add-on
Crawl space foundation walls: spray-foam application sized to local code where crawl space is conditioned

sections.heading: A Tighter Envelope Than Batt or Blown-In Alone
body: The difference between a code-minimum batt-and-blown-in build and a spray-foam-sealed build shows up the first summer the home is occupied. Batt insulation depends on perfect, uncompressed installation around every wire, box, and stud bay to perform at its rated R-value, and blown-in attic insulation does nothing to stop air movement through top-plate gaps, can-light housings, or duct chases. In a climate where roof decks hit 130-150°F and that heat is constantly looking for a path into the conditioned space, those gaps are where AC systems end up working harder than they should for the home's square footage.

Spray foam closes that gap by design. A closed-cell application on the roof deck converts the attic from a vented, heat-soaked space into a sealed, semi-conditioned buffer zone — the difference builders and homeowners in this market actually feel is a smaller, more consistent HVAC load instead of the AC cycling constantly through a 100°F+ afternoon. That's a meaningfully different envelope than one built to hit R-value on a spec sheet alone, and it's the reason builders who want their homes to perform above code (not just pass it) are moving to spray foam as the standard, not the upgrade.

That difference is also a sales conversation. Buyers in this market increasingly ask about summer utility bills before they ask about square footage, and a spray-foam-sealed envelope gives your sales team a concrete answer instead of a generic 'energy efficient' claim. Homes insulated to an above-code standard with a continuous air barrier are strong candidates for Rocky Mountain Power's Wattsmart Homes program and related Dixie Power efficiency incentives, which can be a real talking point for the buyer and, in some cases, a rebate path worth mentioning at the sales table.

sections.heading: Coordinating With Your Framing and HVAC Trades
body: Spray foam application on a new build isn't a standalone trade call — it has to work around framing details and HVAC rough-in placement, and it changes how your HVAC contractor should size the system. When ductwork and equipment sit inside a foam-sealed, conditioned attic instead of a vented one, load calculations and duct sealing requirements shift, and we coordinate directly with your HVAC sub so the assembly is planned correctly rather than discovered as a conflict on-site.

We also flag framing details that affect foam performance before we spray — things like blocking at rim joists, insulation dams at eave vents (if the attic stays vented rather than fully conditioned), and clearances around recessed lighting — so there are no surprises for your inspector or your framing crew after the fact. Because spray foam is the only material we install, we can speak specifically to how a given assembly performs against Zone 3B targets and where it exceeds them — not as a general insulation upsell, but as a specific, code-referenced spec your super or sales team can rely on.

priceFactors.detail: Total conditioned square footage and the mix of roof deck, wall cavity, rim joist, and crawl space square footage all factor into the bid, since closed-cell and open-cell foam price differently.

Open-cell foam (roughly $1.50-$3.00 per sq ft installed) covers standard wall cavities and non-roof-deck attic areas; closed-cell foam (roughly $3.00-$5.00 per sq ft installed) covers roof decks, rim joists, and exterior-adjacent assemblies taking direct heat load.

priceFactors.factor: Number of units and phase scheduling
priceFactors.detail: Multi-lot subdivision phases with a consistent spec across units typically price more efficiently per unit than a single custom build scheduled in isolation.

How cleanly the framing, electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-in trades hand off the unit affects crew time on site — a well-sequenced job moves faster than one with rework or trade conflicts to work around.

faqs.q: Can spray foam meet 2021 IECC Zone 3B code minimums on its own, without batts or blown-in insulation?
faqs.a: Yes. We size closed-cell and open-cell foam thickness specifically to clear Zone 3B R-value targets for each assembly — attic/roof deck, walls, and rim joists — in a single application, with margin above the minimum rather than exactly at it. No other insulation material is layered in.

faqs.q: How does spray foam affect our HVAC design on a new build?
faqs.a: When we seal the roof deck and convert the attic to a conditioned or semi-conditioned space, ductwork and equipment inside that attic are no longer exposed to vented, heat-soaked attic air. That typically allows for tighter HVAC load calculations, but it needs to be planned with your HVAC contractor before installation, not adjusted after the fact — we coordinate that directly.

faqs.q: What point in the build sequence do you install spray foam?
faqs.a: After framing inspection and after electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-in are complete, and before drywall delivery. We work with your superintendent to slot into that window without holding up the schedule.

faqs.q: Do you work on multi-lot subdivision phases or only single custom homes?
faqs.a: Both. We regularly run consistent specs across multi-unit subdivision phases in Washington Fields, Little Valley, Desert Color, and Hurricane's growing subdivisions, as well as one-off custom builds.

faqs.q: Why spec spray foam instead of standard batt-and-blown-in on a spec-built home?
faqs.a: Spray foam's continuous air seal addresses both R-value and air-leakage requirements in one application, which reduces blower-door test failure risk before drywall inspection and gives the finished home a tighter, better-performing envelope against St. George's cooling-load-dominated summers — a meaningful difference for buyers comparing utility bills.
